activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
story:
Autumn sat on the back porch steps at her grandmother's house, holding a folded square of newsprint that her father had pressed into her hands that morning. Relatives milled around the yard with plates of potato salad, and somebody's uncle kept refilling the punch bowl, but Autumn barely looked up. The paper was the obituary, the notice that had run in the town paper about her grandfather's death, and she had read it four times already. It said he was survived by his wife, three children and five grandchildren. It said he had worked thirty years at the hardware store. And in one short line near the bottom, it said that in his youth he had been a sailor, and that he never lost his love of the sea.

A sailor. Grandpa, who got seasick on the ferry to the island, who kept a robust coil of rope in the garage even though he never went on a boat that she knew of. Autumn flipped the paper over, as if the back might explain more, but there was only a coupon for mulch. She had spent whole summers at his kitchen table while he consumed crossword puzzles one clue at a time, and he had never once mentioned the sea. That bothered her more than the sadness did, somehow. A person could hold a whole hidden life and never let it slip.

Melody arrived after lunch with her mother, a plate of lemon bars, and the careful face people wear at these things. "I'm really sorry," she said, sitting down beside Autumn on the step. "Is that him?"

"It's his obituary," Autumn said. "It's a published notice about someone's death, and it has a little account of their life. Family, work, interests. That kind of thing." She tapped the last line. "It says he was a sailor. He never told me that. Not once."

Melody leaned over to read. "Maybe he forgot to tell you. Or maybe he told your dad."

That was the thing to test, Autumn decided. If Grandpa had really loved the sea, there should be evidence somewhere, some trace of it, because a person's interests leak into their stuff whether they talk about them or not. She stood up, brushed crumbs off her skirt, and went inside to the garage. Melody followed.

The garage smelled like oil and old newspaper. Autumn pulled open the bottom drawer of Grandpa's workbench, the one she had always assumed was full of junk. Inside was the coil of rope, tied in a strange, complicated knot she had never seen anywhere else. Beside it lay a brass compass, green with age, and a photograph of a very young man in a sailor's cap standing on a ship's deck, grinning like he had just gotten away with something. It was Grandpa. It was unmistakably Grandpa, fifty years younger.

Autumn carried the photograph out to the yard and found her father by the fence. "You never said he was a sailor," she said.

Her father looked at the picture for a long moment. "He got a concussion falling from the rigging when he was nineteen," he said. "After that he came home and never went back. He didn't like to talk about it." He put his arm around her shoulders. "But he kept everything, didn't he."

Autumn held the photograph up so the light caught the ship's white rail and the boy's crooked grin. "I'm going to learn that knot," she said, and went back for the rope.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: New Zealand voted in a 1993 referendum to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP, and first used it in the 1996 election.
story:
The courthouse hallway smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Riley's knee would not stop bouncing. In twenty minutes his team would stand before a judge in Room 4B and argue that the school's class elections should switch from first-past-the-post to proportional representation, and every team before them had been torn apart by the same question: "Show me one country that actually made the change." Nobody on the judges' panel wanted a theory. They wanted proof.

"We could just make something up," Gurfateh whispered, adjusting the tie he'd borrowed from his uncle, which was roughly the size of a seatbelt. "Judges love confidence."

"They love facts," Naima said. She flipped through their binder one more time, past the sample vote count they'd worked out on pizza night. Under first-past-the-post, their imaginary Class of thirty voters gave the Purple Party eleven seats, even though most people had voted against Purple. Under proportional representation, the seats actually matched the votes. The numbers were right there. It was the missing piece that scared Riley, the country that had done it for real, and it felt like something dormant buried in the back of his brain, waiting for a jolt to wake up.

Flashback to that pizza night: flour on the counter, Naima assigning jobs, Riley insisting he could eat a slice while doing long division. He had knocked over a cup, and while mopping it with his sleeve he'd caught a snippet of a documentary his dad was watching in the next room, something about elections, an island country, a change in how people voted. He hadn't written it down. He'd been too busy discovering that cheese and cartilage don't mix, after biting into something on his slice that his little brother had smuggled in from a science kit. "Ow," he'd said. "That's it. I'm going to look it up later." He never had.

Room 4B's door opened, and Ms. Santos-Reyes, who had driven them to the courthouse and prescribed rest, water, and no arguing in the van, leaned toward them. "Two minutes," she said. "Judges are running ahead of schedule." She did not offer facts or advice. She only straightened Riley's note cards, which were curling like old leaves.

"That documentary," Riley said suddenly, grabbing Naima's sleeve the way Gurfateh's tie grabbed his whole torso. "An island country. New Zealand, maybe? They voted on it. A referendum. And they replaced first-past-the-post with the proportional system. MMP." He wasn't sure. It could have been Australia, or a dream, or a commercial for kiwifruit. Gurfateh was already typing on the ancient tablet they'd brought, and Riley watched the loading bar crawl while the door to 4B opened again and the clerk inside called, "Team four."

"Confirmed," Gurfateh whispered, eyes wide. "New Zealand, 1993 referendum, replaced it. And they first used the new system in the 1996 election." Naima jammed the tablet into Riley's hands and shoved him toward the door.

The judge looked up from her glasses. "Young man, before you begin. Has any real country ever actually switched from first-past-the-post to a proportional system?" Riley held up the tablet, screen still glowing. "Yes, Your Honor. New Zealand. A 1993 referendum to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP. They first used it in the 1996 election." The judge raised one eyebrow, glanced at the screen, and nodded slowly. "Proceed."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega.
story:
Alexis crouched beside the workbench in Mr. Ivanova's garage, staring at the multimeter in her hand. On the little screen, next to the number, sat a symbol that looked exactly like a tiny horseshoe. "Why does it say my wire has three horseshoes?" she asked.

Sarah laughed from the doorway. "It doesn't. That's not a horseshoe." But she wouldn't say what it was, which Sarah seemed to think was hilarious. Behind her, Aidan shifted the toolbox he was carrying and checked the clock on the wall. "Twelve minutes," he said. "The science fair judges start at ten sharp."

The premise of their project was simple: prove that a thin wire had more resistance than a thick one. Alexis's job was the measuring, and the measuring had to be done right now, because Mr. Ivanova needed his garage back at ten for a repair job. The meters, the spools of wire, the whole table had to be cleared out. Alexis clipped the meter leads onto the first wire, read the numbers, and wrote them in her notebook. Voltage. Current. But the horseshoe symbol kept showing up beside every reading, and she could not shake the feeling that it mattered.

"It's the omega symbol," Sarah finally said, bouncing on her heels. Sarah wanted credit for the answer, Alexis could tell, wanted to be the one who got to say it. "Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega." She said it slowly, like she was handing over a prize.

Alexis looked at the screen again. Three ohms. Then it clicked into place, the whole hidden chain of it: the meter could not show her resistance directly, but it could show voltage and current, and if she divided one by the other, the answer would come out in those little omegas. She had been treating the symbol like decoration when it was the key to the entire calculation. She grabbed her pencil and worked through the thin wire: six volts, two amps. Three ohms. The meter agreed with her arithmetic, and her stomach did a small flip.

"Now the thick one," Aidan said. Eight minutes. He held the wire steady while she clipped the leads on, and his elbow knocked a spool off the bench. It rolled under the freezer. Neither of them moved for a second, then Alexis lunged for it while Sarah read out the numbers, fast: "Four point five volts, three amps!" Alexis divided on the fly, one point five, and scribbled it down as the spool came back up in her hand, dusty and cold.

They packed the table in the last four minutes, stacking boxes against the garage wall while Mr. Ivanova watched with his arms crossed and the hood of a car already popped open behind him. Alexis taped her notebook page to the display board, the two omegas side by side like trophies. Sarah tapped the little horseshoe shape with one finger.

"Still looks like a horseshoe to me," Sarah said.

"Then it's the luckiest horseshoe in the whole garage," Alexis said, and she carried the board out into the sunlight.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Motion sickness happens when the eyes and the balance organs in the inner ear send the brain conflicting signals about whether the body is moving.
story:
The back seat of the van smelled like sunscreen and granola bars, and James had his comic open on his knees even though the road through the national park kept curving. His stomach had been complaining since the second switchback. He read one panel, then another, and the queasy feeling climbed from his belly to his throat like water rising in a glass.

"Put that thing down," said Shay, who was squished in beside him with her hiking boots on the cooler. "You look like a pickle."

"I'm fine," James said, and immediately regretted it, because the van swung around another bend and his stomach swung the other way. He stared at the page. The drawings wobbled. That was strange, he thought. The drawings weren't moving. The van was moving, and his stomach seemed to know it, but his eyes were telling his brain that he was sitting still, staring at paper. Two different messages, arriving at the same time. He shut the comic and looked out the window instead, at the far ridge where a line of elk stood in the morning light. The queasiness didn't vanish, but it stopped climbing.

"I figured it out," he announced. "Reading in the car makes me sick because my eyes say I'm not moving, but the balance parts inside my ears say I am. The two signals don't match."

"That's actually a thing," Shay said. "My mom calls it conflicting signals. Eyes and ears disagreeing." She leaned over him to look at the elk. "They migrate through this valley every fall, the ranger said. Whole herds of them."

Last summer flashed into James's mind, sharp and embarrassing. He'd been on the ferry to visit his grandmother, reading in the cabin while the water outside turned choppy, and he'd spent the whole trip with his head on a table while his cousin played cards. Everyone said it was the boat's fault. But the boat had been fine. It was the book, all along. He'd been testing the wrong idea for a year.

The van rolled into the trailhead parking lot beside a river that ran fast and turbulent over pale rocks, white water stacking up in little standing waves. A notice board near the path said something about a controversy over reopening an old trail, and Shay's dad paused to read it while the kids stretched their legs. James took a slow breath of pine-smelling air. His stomach had settled almost completely. He looked back at the van, then at the trail climbing toward the ridge, and he reached into his pocket and left the comic rolled up on the seat.

"Coming?" Shay called, already three steps up the path.

"Right behind you," James said, and followed her into the trees.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
story:
The stall smelled of basil and wet dirt. Emile set his bag of onions and garlic on the table while Mr. Tesfaye sharpened a knife on a little steel rod, the sound like a zipper going fast.

"Today you make the sauce," Mr. Tesfaye said. "First, the claw. Curl your fingertips under, like this, and let your knuckles guide the blade. The knife can't bite what it can't reach."

Emile curled his fingers and pressed the onion half flat side down. He cut slowly, and the pieces came off almost symmetrical, small white squares. He remembered last Saturday, when his first batch of sauce had turned out wrong. He had dumped the garlic in with the onions, cranked the heat, and gone to find the salt. When he came back, the kitchen smelled sharp and burnt. The sauce had tasted bitter, and he had eaten his pasta anyway because throwing it out felt like admitting the whole evening was wasted.

He thought about that batch now. The onions had been fine. They were soft and sweet by the time the garlic was black. It wasn't the pan or the salt. The garlic was the part that had changed. Garlic burns much faster than onion, and burnt garlic tastes bitter. That had to be it. So the fix was simple: the garlic goes in only after the onions have softened.

"Oil in, onions first," he said. The camp stove hissed under the pot Mr. Tesfaye kept at the stall for demonstrations. Emile stirred the onions and watched them go from stiff and white to soft and translucent at the edges. Then he pushed them to one side, tipped the minced garlic into the empty spot, and stirred for maybe thirty seconds, no more.

Shaun, who had wandered over from the honey stall, leaned in. "Smells different from your last one."

"Last one I burnt the garlic," Emile said. He paraphrased his own rule as he stirred: onions get a head start, garlic gets the last minute. That was all there was to it.

Mr. Tesfaye tasted the sauce from a wooden spoon. "Good. Now the basil, torn, not cut."

Emile tore the leaves and dropped them in. "Do I have to stir it a certain way?"

"No obligation at all," Mr. Tesfaye said, handing him the spoon. "Just taste it."

Emile lifted the spoon and blew on it.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In American English, a quotation inside another quotation uses single quotation marks within the double ones.
story:
Ryan stared at the blinking cursor and wrote the same sentence for the fourth time. "I'm stuck," he said, sliding his draft across the library table to Gillian. "Mr. Lin says my dialogue is a mess, and he's right. Every time a character talks, I just guess."

Gillian picked up the paper and squinted at it. "Here's your problem. Your character Dana says, and then you've got quotation marks inside quotation marks, and it looks like a bird walked across the page." She tapped one smudged line. "What is Dana even saying?"

"She's repeating something," Ryan said. "Like, Dana tells her friend, 'My brother said, "Stop hogging the pancakes."' I don't know which marks go where. And honestly, my whole story is just people talking about breakfast. There's no ending. Mr. Lin wrote 'Where's the climax?' in red pen, like it's obvious."

Gillian set the paper down. "My brother complains about this every single time he edits the school paper. In American English, he says, a quotation inside another quotation uses single quotation marks within the double ones. He made me repeat it at dinner until I could say it backwards." She grabbed a pencil, flipped Ryan's draft over, and wrote the sentence out clean: Dana said, "My brother told me, 'Stop hogging the pancakes.'" The single marks sat inside the doubles like a nut inside a shell.

Ryan copied it onto his own paper, then tested it. He wrote another line where Dana's friend answered, "He actually said, 'Make the pancakes nutritious, at least,'" and checked it against Gillian's example. The pattern held. He flipped to a page in a library memoir he'd been reading for fun, a woman writing about her loud family kitchen, and found the same marks doing the same job. "It's everywhere," he said, almost triumphant. "Once you see it, you can't stop seeing it."

"Great. Now fix your climax," Gillian said. "What's the worst thing that could happen to Dana?"

Ryan thought about it while the radiator clanked and somebody's sneakers squeaked past the study carrels. His story had been people chatting, nothing at stake. He bent over the desk and wrote fast: the pancake fight escalates, Dana's brother flings the last plate, it shatters, and in the sudden quiet Dana says, "Mom told me this morning, 'You two would thrive on chaos,' and she was right." He underlined the line twice.

He read the new ending aloud in a low voice, one finger under each word, checking the marks as he went. Double outside, single inside, period tucked in where it belonged. It looked like real writing now, the kind with pages you'd actually turn. He straightened the pages, squared the corners, and carried the draft across the library to where Mr. Lin was shelving books.

"Better?" Ryan asked, holding it out.

Mr. Lin read the last paragraph, and one corner of his mouth lifted. "Read me the pancake line again," he said.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
story:
The regional meet started in forty minutes, and Norah still didn't have a plan for the eight hundred metres. She sat on the metal bench by lane one, turning her race number over in her hands. On the back, in pencil, she had written the math she'd worked out at breakfast: eight hundred metres, three minutes, on a four-hundred-metre track. Two laps. She divided the time by the laps and wrote the answer twice, then circled it. Ninety seconds per lap. To finish in three minutes, she had to average ninety seconds each time around.

Frederick dropped onto the bench beside her, breathing hard from his own warm-up. "What's all that?" he asked, leaning over to see the number.

"My lap target," Norah said. "Ninety seconds. If I go faster than that on the first lap, I'm borrowing from the second one, and I always die at the two hundred mark. Every race, same spot."

"So don't go out fast," Frederick said, which sounded logical but wasn't an actual plan. Norah wanted numbers, not advice. Last month she had sprinted the first lap in seventy-eight seconds and then crawled home in over a hundred and ten. The pattern was there, but she couldn't see it while running. She needed something she could check during the race itself.

A mosquito landed on Frederick's arm and he slapped it. "Little parasite," he muttered, rubbing the spot. Norah pulled the stopwatch her mother had lent her out of her shoe bag. "Will you time my first lap?" she asked. "Stand at the line and call it out. If I'm faster than ninety, I'll slow down on the back straight. That's the test." Frederick agreed, and they walked to the start, gravel crunching under their shoes, the sun already warm on the white lanes.

Ms. Park, the starter, checked their numbers and said the eight-hundred metre heat would go in ten minutes. Norah toed the line,心跳 steady. When the gun cracked, she held herself back even as three girls pulled ahead. At the line she heard Frederick shout, "Ninety-one!" Right on target. She kept the same rhythm past the two hundred mark, the place where her legs usually turned to rope, and this time they held.

Rounding the final bend, she was still passing people. She crossed the line, bent over, hands on knees, gasping. The clock read 3:01. Frederick waved the stopwatch at her from the fence. "Second lap, ninety-two," he called. "Almost even." Norah looked up, still breathing hard, and grinned. "Next race, I'm writing the numbers on my hand."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
story:
Benjamin stood in the parking lot of the community food bank on Saturday morning, staring at a battered blue truck with a logo he half recognized. "I've seen that symbol before," he said, mostly to himself. Leela, who had talked him into volunteering, slid a crate of canned beans toward him. "Then stop staring and start carrying." The truck's door was dented and the warehouse behind it was so dilapidated that half the letters had fallen off the BUILDING BETTER COMMUNITIES sign, but the logo itself was crisp: a bowl with rays coming off it, and the words FEEDING AMERICA.

Inside, Ms. Mercado handed him a clipboard and put him in charge of sorting donations by date. It was the kind of job where you could let your mind wander, so his kept drifting back to the truck. Last summer, at his cousin's place two states away, he had watched a food distribution in a church parking lot. Those boxes had come off a truck with a bowl logo too. He had assumed the two places just happened to pick the same clipart. Now the assumption bothered him. Small food banks in different states usually had no budget for design, and anyway, two places choosing the identical symbol by chance felt like too much of a coincidence. Maybe, he thought, the logo meant the places were connected somehow, the way a jersey tells you which team a player belongs to.

He decided to test it. In the loading bay, trucks came and went all morning, and he began asking each driver one question: where did your truck start today? A man from the local pantry said right here. A woman said she'd driven in from a warehouse across the county. Every single truck, from every direction, carried the bowl. When the last driver climbed down, Benjamin pointed at his door. "Why do all of you have that same logo, even though you're from different cities?" The driver grinned. "Because we're all part of Feeding America. It's a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks, all across the United States."

Leela, stacking boxes nearby, raised an eyebrow with visible skepticism. "More than two hundred? He's just a driver, he could be guessing." So they went looking for proof instead of arguing. In the office, Ms. Mercado let them peek at a folder of shipment paperwork, and there it was again and again, the same letterhead, banks shipping to other banks, boxes moving from city to city like beads on one long string. Benjamin tried to condense what he'd seen into a single sentence for his notes and couldn't; it kept turning into three.

At the end of the shift, Leela nudged him. "Okay, I was wrong. It's not a coincidence, it's a system." Benjamin peeled off his volunteer sticker and stuck it to the folder as a bookmark for next time. "Same time next Saturday?" he asked, and Ms. Mercado tossed him the clipboard from across the room.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
story:
Natalie pulled her coat around her shoulders, trying to insulate herself against the cold air rushing through the gap under the stadium seats, while her dad argued with Uncle Marco two rows down. The game on the field hadn't even started yet, but the real contest was already happening in Section 12.

"I'm telling you, Argentina won the first World Cup," Uncle Marco insisted. "It was their whole thing back then."

"Argentina? No way," her dad shot back. "I'm almost positive it was Brazil."

Natalie frowned. She had no idea who was right, but she noticed something both of them had missed. "Wait," she said, standing up so they could hear her. "You're not even sure of the year. How can you argue about the winner if you don't know when it was?"

"Everyone knows when," Uncle Marco said, waving a hand. "It was old times. Nineteen-something."

Natalie sat back down next to Mckayla, who was sharing her blanket. "Want to help me settle this?" she asked. "There has to be a program in the gift bag." Mckayla dug through the paper bag of souvenirs and pulled out the glossy game program. Somewhere in there, Natalie figured, a stadium celebrating soccer history might mention its own beginnings. She flipped past pictures of players and a page about the local economy recovering after the recession, which she skipped, until she found a timeline printed along the bottom of a history spread.

"Here it is," she said, running her finger down the page. "The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930. And Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final."

"Four to two," Mckayla repeated, peering at the tiny print to double-check. "You were both wrong, and one of you was extra wrong."

Uncle Marco climbed the two rows to see for himself, and his shoulders dropped. "Uruguay. Huh." He read it aloud one more time, slowly, like he was memorizing it for future arguments.

Her dad laughed and handed his brother a foam finger, the one shaped like the number one. "You have to wear this now," he said. "For being the most confidently wrong."

"That's not the deal we made," Uncle Marco protested, but he put it on anyway, and soon everyone around them was laughing too, even the grandmother in the next row who had been watching the whole thing like a referee.

Before kickoff, the stadium screen showed an eagle from the local rescue center, part of an ad about endangered wildlife. "Look at that," Mckayla said quietly, and Natalie turned to see it just as the bird spread its wings across the giant screen.

Then the whistle blew, and the whole section jumped to its feet, foam finger and all.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
story:
Harper set the microscope on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and her half-eaten toast and peeled a paper-thin layer off the onion her dad had left on the counter. The layer was so thin it almost vanished when she held it up to the window. That was the point, according to the worksheet Mr. Ross had handed out on Friday. Thin enough for light to pass through, he had said, and clear enough to see one cell from the next. Harper's problem was bigger than thinness, though. She had exactly one weekend to draw and label a cell wall, a cell membrane, and a nucleus, and last night she had gotten nothing but a gray blur.

Abigaelle arrived at ten with her own onion in a plastic bag, because her mother believed in backups. "Did you figure out the magnification thing?" she asked, dropping her bag on a chair. "Elliott says we only get fifty times, so the nucleus is basically invisible, so we should just draw it from the textbook and call it done."

"That's cheating," Harper said, though she had considered it for about ten minutes in the dark last night, lying there weighing it: a perfect drawing copied from a book against a messy one she had actually seen. She had decided the messy one, but only barely, and she still wasn't sure she'd choose the same way twice.

They put the onion skin on a slide, added one drop of water, and pressed down the cover slip. Harper turned the microscope's smallest lens into place and leaned in. There they were: rows of brick-shaped cells, neat as a garden wall. She could draw the outer edge of each brick and label it the cell wall, no problem. But the membrane hugging the inside of the wall was a whisper of a line, and the nucleus was nowhere.

"Fifty times," Abigaelle said, squinting through the eyepiece. "That's what Elliott told me. Tiny."

Harper sat back. "Where did he get fifty?" She picked up the microscope and turned it over, the way she'd flip a puzzle box to look for the picture on the back. Printed on the eyepiece, in letters small enough to hide from a careless eye, was "10x." On the lens barrel it said "4x." She did the math in the fog on the window with her finger. Ten times four was forty, not fifty, and even forty wasn't the whole story. She clicked the next lens around, the one marked "10x," and computed again: eyepiece power times objective power, ten times ten, a hundred. The last lens said "40x," which came to four hundred.

"Four hundred times," she said. "Elliott multiplied wrong, or never multiplied at all. It's the eyepiece times the objective." She said it out loud mostly to fix it in her own head, because she had almost believed him, and that bothered her. She had accepted a number without checking it, the way she used to copy her sister's homework answers in fourth grade, and that habit had cost her a whole unit on fractions before she'd caught it.

She cranked the stage up, focused slowly, and there it was: a darker dot inside one of the bricks, steady and small, like a pebble resting in a clear stream. The nucleus. The membrane showed itself as a faint border just inside the wall once she knew what to look for. Abigaelle leaned in and gasped, and for a minute neither of them said anything.

They were still drawing when Elliott texted to ask if they'd finished from the book. Harper photographed the eyepiece view, zoomed so even her dad's phone could show the nucleus, and typed back, "Come over. Bring your own onion. We'll show you the real thing, four hundred times." Then she picked up her pencil and drew the last label, pressing hard enough to make sure it would still be there Monday.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Arthur had never played real soccer before, and the first practice at Riverside Park left him feeling suspiciously great. He had run drills for two hours, chased a boy named Caelan all over the field, and even scored once on a scrambled rebound. Walking home, he decided the whole thing had been easy. Maybe the coach was being soft because it was only the first week, or maybe the drills Mr. Bondarenko enforced, the sprinting kind, were not really that hard.

The next morning his legs felt fine. "See you at the park," he texted Caelan, adding a muscle emoji, which turned out to be a mistake. By second period, climbing the stairs to math class, his thighs began to ache. By afternoon he had to lower himself onto chairs like an old man. "What did you do to yourself?" Kinsley asked, watching him grip the desk to stand up.

"Nothing," Arthur said. "That's the weird part. It started today, and practice was yesterday." He turned the timing over in his head while Kinsley laughed at him. It did not make sense. If the running had hurt him, it should have hurt right after, like a bruise. Instead there had been a whole day of feeling fine, then this. He remembered his older cousin once describing something with a long name, and that evening he looked it up on his mother's phone, holding it with aching arms. The screen said muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks twenty-four to seventy-two hours later, not right away, and that it had a name.

"Delayed onset muscle soreness," Arthur announced at the park the next day, before Caelan could even say hello. "That's what I've got." He demonstrated by attempting a squat and stopping halfway down, wobbling. "So Saturday will be worse than today, probably. Sunday maybe still bad. And then it should fade." In a vain attempt to seem tough, he tried a slow jog to the goal and back, and had to stop and press his palms against his knees.

Mr. Bondarenko blew the whistle and gathered them in the usual hierarchy, team captain first, newcomers last, Arthur somewhere near the end of the line. "Take it easy today," the coach said. "First week always catches up with you." Arthur thought about his first walk home, how sure he had been that soccer was going to be easy, and how wrong that had been. He rolled his ankle in the cool grass, waiting. "Caelan," he called out, "if I can't walk by Sunday, you're carrying my bag."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Nicotine's effects fade quickly because the body clears about half of it in roughly two hours, so users soon feel the urge for another dose.
story:
Mya sat in the dentist's waiting room with her older cousin, turning a stack of index cards over in her lap. On the cards were notes for her health presentation on Friday: nicotine, dopamine, the brain's reward pathway. She had the words written down, but she didn't think she could actually explain them yet, not out loud, not without reading.

"Can I practice on you?" she asked her cousin.

"Sure," he said, and glanced at the clock on the wall behind the receptionist.

Mya started in. "So nicotine gets into the brain and tricks the reward pathway, the same system that makes food taste worth finding again. It pushes out dopamine, the chemical that says this is good, do it again. That's how addiction starts." Her cousin nodded, but he was tapping his foot against the chair leg. Three minutes later he said he'd be right back and went out to the parking lot. Mya checked the time on her phone: 3:42.

She read two more index cards and waited. When he came back he seemed calmer, and he even helped her with a line. "Say it like you're telling a story," he said. "Start with what happens first." Mya rewrote her opening, and when the dental assistant called a man named Mr. Ba through the door, she barely noticed. At 5:38 her cousin went out to the lot again. Mya looked at her phone and did the math. She leaned over and confided in him quietly, "It's been almost two hours. It was almost two hours last time, too."

He rubbed the back of his neck. "Yeah. That's about when it wears off. Your body gets rid of half of what's in you in around two hours, so you start wanting more. That's the whole thing."

"And your brain learned to want it because the pathway tagged it as good," Mya said. "Like a bias toward doing it again."

"If you want to call it that," her cousin said.

When Katelyn and Ronald came in for Ronald's appointment, Mya was still holding the phone with the times on the screen. "You two are my test audience," she said. She gave the whole explanation in ninety seconds, the reward pathway, the dopamine, the fading that sends users looking for another dose every couple of hours. Katelyn said, "That was actually clear," and Ronald asked one question about the pathway that Mya answered from her cards.

The receptionist called her cousin's name for his cleaning. He stood, pointed at her cards, and said, "Ninety seconds. Friday. Don't read."

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: In the side-angle-side rule the angle must be the included angle, the one between the two given sides; two sides and a different angle do not always prove congruence.
story:
The tutoring centre on Miller Street had a smell of dry-erase markers and old carpet, and a sign-up sheet so sparse that Levi's name appeared twice because the owner had forgotten he'd come Monday. Mr. Reyes ran the place like a man who had once planned to be an entrepreneur and had settled for three whiteboards and a coffee machine that only made decaf. Levi was there because his geometry test had come back with a big red circle around problem four.

He had written: side, angle, side, therefore congruent. Mr. Reyes had written one word beside it: "Which angle?" Levi hadn't understood the question. There were three angles. He'd picked one.

At the table by the window, Kylie spread out her own test, which had a check on the same problem. "Look," she said, turning it toward him. Her two marked sides met at a corner, and her marked angle sat right there in the hinge between them. Levi looked at his own paper. His sides were AB and BC, and his angle was angle A, off at the end, wedged between a marked side and an unmarked one.

"So that's it? Mine's in the wrong spot?" He took out a ruler and sketched two triangles, each with the same two sides and the same angle at the tip, the angle not between the sides. The triangles came out different, like two doors open to different widths even though the hinges matched. He sketched Kylie's version next, sides pinching the angle between them, and the triangles snapped together like copies. "The angle has to be the included angle," he said. "The one between the two sides. If it's a different angle, it doesn't always work." He said it twice, once for the room and once for himself, and Kylie nodded like a judge.

That night he sent Mr. Reyes a message, because the test rewrite was Friday and he wanted to be sure. "Dear Mr. Reyes," he typed. "Problem four. I used sides AB and BC but I marked angle A. Angle A is not between those sides. Angle B is the included angle. If I redo the proof with angle B, is that the fix, or did I break something else too? Also the coffee machine is out of cups again. Levi." He read it over, deleted the part about the coffee machine, put it back, and hit send.

The reply came at 9:40: "That's the fix. Bring a cup." Friday, Levi rewrote problem four, marked angle B, and slid it across the table. Mr. Reyes read it, drew a checkmark slow enough to seem ceremonial, and pointed at the coffee machine. Levi went to get the cup.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings, which is why many museums keep delicate items in dim rooms.
story:
The bus dropped Parker's class at the nature reserve just after nine. Ms. Swampy handed out clipboards and told everyone they would sketch one thing in the visitor center and one thing on the trail. Parker wanted the old quilt hanging in the back room, because his grandmother had one with the same star pattern, and he planned to draw every color exactly.

The quilt room was so dim he could barely tell the reds from the browns. Karlee stood beside him with her arms crossed. "This is ridiculous," she said. "How are we supposed to sketch anything in the dark?" A guide passing through the doorway heard her and paused. "Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper, and some paintings, so we keep the delicate things in dim rooms," she said, and moved on toward the bird feeders.

Parker copied the shapes as best he could, but he kept thinking about what the guide said. On the trail, the group stopped at a small information kiosk where a cloth banner hung in full sun, printed with the reserve's green leaf logo. Parker compared it to a stack of flyers inside the kiosk case, out of the light. The banner's green had gone pale and washed out, almost yellow-green, while the flyers were still dark. The sun was doing to the banner exactly what the guide had described.

He told Aaryan about it at lunch. "So the dim room isn't a mistake," Parker said. "It's protecting the quilt." Aaryan raised an eyebrow with clear skepticism, so Parker generated a plan on the spot. He borrowed two sheets of colored paper from Ms. Swampy's supply bag, taped one to the sunny window of the activity cabin, and kept the other in his clipboard, flat under his sketch. "It's only temporary," he said. "We'll check after the afternoon walk."

When the class came back to the cabin for closing circle, Parker peeled the paper off the window. Nothing had changed, and he admitted it. "Right, the fading is slow," he said. "The quilt took years, not one afternoon. But the banner still proves it happens." Ms. Swampy looked at the two identical sheets, then at the pale banner by the kiosk, and gave a small nod.

On the bus, Parker taped his sketch of the quilt beside the flyer's bright green leaf. "One from the dark room," he said, "one from the light." Karlee leaned over the seat and tapped the quilt drawing. "Now draw me the star part," she said.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
story:
Cooper lay on the living room couch under a quilt that smelled like lemon tea, staring at the water stain on the ceiling. It was Saturday, day two of the flu, and Samantha's birthday party started at three. His fever had finally dropped, his throat no longer felt like he had swallowed an arid desert wind, and he had already texted his mom from the couch, which she could see from the kitchen, because walking seemed like too much effort.

"I'm better," he called. "I want to go."

She came in and put the back of her hand against his forehead. "You're cooler, but you're not going."

A hot knot of resentment formed in his chest. He was going to miss the cake, the backyard games, everything, just because he felt slightly tired. He pulled his phone from under the quilt and opened a message to Ilyas, who had already said he was going.

"Tell me exactly what happens," Cooper typed. "Every detail." Then, because that wasn't enough, he opened the internet and searched his own question: can you go to a party after the flu gets better. The first thing that came up was from the CDC, the big health agency his science teacher was always citing. He read the line twice. People with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness. He checked the calendar app. Fever had started Thursday evening. Thursday, Friday, Saturday. That made today day two.

So feeling better didn't mean much. He could still be carrying the thing that made him miserable, ready to migrate from his sneeze to Samantha or Ilyas or half the class, and they would all be flattened next weekend. He scrolled down, looking for a loophole, but the line just sat there, plain as the water stain.

His mom came back with soup. "You're sulking," she said.

"I'm not sulking. I'm calculating." He turned the phone toward her. "Read that."

She read it, and her eyebrows went up a little, like she was seeing him do actual math. "Huh. So when could you go?"

"Monday, technically. Which helps nothing, because the party is today." He pulled the quilt up to his chin. "Tell Samantha the party should migrate to next weekend. It's the only fair solution."

His mom laughed, sat down on the arm of the couch, and dialed Samantha's number, holding the phone out so Cooper could hear it ring.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
story:
The argument was going when Kate walked into Claira's kitchen, and it had clearly been going for a while. Claira's older brother held out his phone, jabbing at the screen. "It's white and gold, Claira. Look at it. Look."

"It's blue and black," Claira said, slowly and dangerously, the way people talk when they've said something ten times already. "I have looked. It is blue and black."

"Maybe your screen is broken," said their dad, leaning in. He frowned. Then he blinked. "Huh. White and gold."

"Dad!"

"I'm sorry! It's white and gold!"

Kate took the phone, because that seemed like the polite thing to do, and because she wanted to see whatever could make a family shout at each other over a photo of a dress. The dress on the screen was pale and shimmery, with darker trim. She turned to Claira. "It's blue and black."

Claira threw her arms around her. "THANK you. Kate, you are the only sane person in this house."

But Claira's brother snatched the phone back and squinted at Kate like she was lying on purpose. "You're just taking her side." He dismissed her answer with a flick of his hand, as if Claira had paid her off, which Kate thought was unfair. She wasn't taking sides. She was reporting what her eyes did.

They escaped to Claira's room, where Huxley was already sprawled on the rug building something out of polymer clay, a little lopsided dragon with wings like melted spoons. Kate showed him the photo on Claira's brother's phone, which Claira had smuggled upstairs under her hoodie.

"White and gold," Huxley said instantly. He held up the dragon. "Does he look white and gold too?"

"No, he looks like a failed experiment."

"He is NOT a failed experiment."

Claira flopped backward onto her bed. "How can we all look at the same photo and see different colors? That's terrifying. What else are we seeing wrong?"

Kate sat down beside the clay dragon and thought about it. If it were just one person being weird, that would be one thing, but the house was split clean down the middle, and the dad had switched. So maybe it wasn't the photo. Maybe it was the people. She had an idea, and it was testable. "Don't tell them what I said," she told Huxley. "We're going to show people the photo with no hints and write down every answer."

She texted her mom: "Show the dress photo to everyone at work. Don't say anything first. Just write me what each person sees." An hour later her mom replied: "Grandma says white and gold. Mr. Petrov says blue and black. The cashier said white and gold, then looked again, said blue and black, and got upset. What are you doing to us."

"See," Kate said, showing Huxley and Claira the messages. "Half and half. Everywhere. Same photo." That evening Claira's aunt arrived for dinner, and when Kate slid the phone across the table, the aunt said blue and black, then demanded to know why everyone was grinning at her. Kate kept her list in her notebook, feeling like a scientist, even if she couldn't say why it happened.

Later, Claira's brother found Kate in the hallway and held out the phone one more time, almost shyly. "Blue and black," he admitted. "It switched for me after dinner. The real dress is blue and black, I looked it up." He shrugged. "I still say the lighting makes it look white and gold."

"So we're both right about what we see," Kate said, "and wrong about each other."

He nodded slowly, like that was the strangest thing anyone had said to him all day, and then went downstairs to tell his dad, and Kate heard him say, at the bottom of the stairs, "Dad. You have to look again."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way.
story:
The living room smelled like burnt popcorn and salsa, because Dad had tried to make both at the same time. Addison claimed the good spot on the couch early, tucked between Gaelle and Lianna, while Mr. Pelletier from next door settled into the armchair with a bowl of chips balanced on his knee like a crown. On the screen, the stadium roared, and the whole room roared with it, since the game had gone to extra innings.

Addison was only half watching the score. She was counting. "Gaelle," she whispered, "look at the numbers on their backs." Every time the camera panned across the dugout she scanned the jerseys, hunting for one number in particular: 42. The shortstop wore 7. The reliever wore 31. She checked the outfield, the bullpen, even the guys warming up on the side. Nobody, on either team, wore 42.

"Maybe it's unlucky," Lianna said, dunking a chip so aggressively it snapped in half.

"Like a curse? Or a virus that spreads through the whole league?" Addison said. It did seem like a plague of missing numbers. She grabbed her phone and typed fast, thumbs flying. The first result made her sit up straight. In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. She read the next line twice. It was the first time any professional athlete had ever been honored that way. Not just one team, every team. Nobody anywhere could wear it again.

"Wait, like a jersey that got sick?" Gaelle said, frowning.

"No, retired, like the number got promoted and doesn't have to work anymore," Addison said, and Lianna snorted soda through her nose.

"Hey," Mr. Pelletier said, pointing his chip at her. "Grandpa, explain," Addison said before he could start, and he laughed, because he knew the rule in this house was that she found things out herself. She held up her phone instead and he nodded slowly, like she'd passed some kind of secret test.

Then came the twist. When the game finally ended and everyone stretched, Dad reached up and took down the old framed jersey that had hung above the TV since Addison was little. The fabric was frail at the shoulders, yellowed at the collar, and stitched across the back, in thread gone soft with age, was a big number 42. She had looked at that jersey a thousand times without ever once seeing it.

"That was your great-grandfather's," Dad said. "He played in the minors the same year Robinson broke in. Kept the jersey his whole life."

Addison touched the glass over the number. "Every player on that field tonight," she said, "and not one of them can wear what's hanging in our living room."

Mr. Pelletier raised his chip in salute. "Kid," he said, "you elaborate better than the announcers do."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
story:
The gym smelled like hot glue and burnt coffee, and the robotics competition started in forty minutes. Victor sat cross-legged behind his team's table, laptop balanced on a folding chair, typing as fast as his fingers would let him. The judge would walk around and ask each team to run a program on the spot, and this year Mr. Lin had required every program to be written in Python. Victor's job was the prime number checker: type in a number, and the screen should say whether it was prime.

"It keeps saying 2 is not prime," Victor said. "Two. That has to be prime. That's like the most prime number there is."

Jaiden leaned over from the soldering mat, squinting at the screen. "Then your code's lying to you."

"It's not lying. It's doing exactly what I told it to do, that's the problem." Victor scrolled up through the loop he had written, his stomach tightening. Somewhere in those lines was a mistake he couldn't see, and the judges would see it in about half an hour.

Damon wandered over with a half-eaten granola bar. "What if you just make it print prime for 2? Like, special case it."

"That's a bandage," Victor said. "If I don't find the real cause, it'll happen again with some other number and I won't know why." He thought about Mr. Lin's voice from last week: debugging is systematic work. Don't guess. Test one thing, then the next. So Victor grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote the numbers he had tried in a column: 7, prime. 9, not prime. 11, prime. 2, not prime. The pattern sat there like a magic trick, and magic tricks, his father always said, were never magic, only an illusion. Something hidden was doing the work.

He read his loop out loud, slowly, walking his finger along the line. For every divisor from 2 up to the number itself, check if it divides evenly. Then it hit him. When the number was 2, the loop checked whether 2 divided 2, and of course it did, evenly, every single time. The program took that as proof of not prime. He covered his mouth. "It's checking the number against itself."

"So?" Damon said.

"So I have to stop before that." Victor deleted one character, changed the range, and ran it again. He typed 2 and hit enter, and the screen said prime. He tried 4. Not prime. He tried 6, then 8, and both came back not prime, which made sense to him now in a way it hadn't before. "Damon," he said, "2 is the only even prime number. Every even number bigger than 2 can be divided evenly by 2, so none of them are prime. Only 2 gets to be both."

Damon blinked. "Huh. That's kind of lonely."

"Try to replicate it," Jaiden said, pointing at the screen. "Break it again on purpose. That's how you know."

So Victor typed a 9 and watched it say not prime, and then a 13, and then, because his hands were shaking a little from the coffee he wasn't supposed to have, a 97. Prime. Prime. Prime. Down the row, Mr. Lin clapped his hands and called, "Five minutes, judges are starting at table one."

Victor hit save, closed the laptop halfway, and held his breath.

"Table three," Mr. Lin called out, "you're next."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of 60 means one beat each second.
story:
Grandpa's piano sat in the front room like a polite old elephant, and Noah had been warned not to bother it, which meant he thought about nothing else. His mom dropped him off every Tuesday with a snack and a warning, and every Tuesday he lifted the fallboard and plunked out the first six notes of the piece Mr. Crowchild, his band teacher, had assigned. The trouble was the sheet music. At the top it said "Andante, quarter note equals 60," and then halfway down the page it demanded "f," and later "pp," and at the bottom it shouted "Accelerando!" Noah could read the notes fine. The other stuff felt like instructions written in invisible ink.

"Your grandpa has a metronome somewhere," said Abygael when Noah complained about it at school. She played clarinet and treated every problem like a scavenger hunt. "Mine's shaped like a lemon."

"There's a metronome," Kya said, "and there's a clock, and they're not the same thing, so stop texting about it." She was helping her uncle rebuild a generator in his garage that weekend, and she had declared herself an expert on anything mechanical, including, apparently, pianos.

On Saturday, both of them came over, and the three of them searched the house. They found a drawer of unmatched socks, a puzzle missing its border pieces, and a tin of butterscotch candies so old they had fused into one candy. No metronome. But above the piano hung a wall clock with a second hand, and Noah stopped staring at the sheet music long enough to stare at that instead.

"Wait," he said. "Sixty. If the tempo is sixty, then a beat is one every second. Like that." He pointed at the second hand ticking around. "Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so sixty means one beat each second."

"Then play with the clock," Abygael said, mouth full of fused butterscotch. "Be the clock's apprentice."

So Noah set his left hand on his knee and tapped once every time the second hand jumped. He felt like a robot at first, then like a drummer, then like neither, and finally like a guy who was simply slow on purpose. The piece sounded different. It had room in it. When the page said "f," he leaned in and made it loud, and when it said "pp" he played so softly that Kya complained she couldn't hear, and he said that was the entire point, and she threw a sofa cushion at him.

They argued about the accelerando. Kya insisted it meant "get faster immediately, like a generator spinning up." Abygael said no, it meant gradually, or the word would be "surprise." Noah appointed the wall clock as the impartial judge and began tapping along with it, then drifting ahead, one second, then a little less than a second per beat, until the ticking and his hand disagreed like old friends.

From the kitchen doorway, Grandpa watched with a mug of tea, and when Noah finished, wobbling but upright, Grandpa tapped his mug against the doorframe and said, "Encore. But this time, the loud part louder."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Lowering the coverslip onto the slide at an angle, one edge first, helps push out air so fewer bubbles form over the cells.
story:
Simon had exactly ten minutes before Mr. Goldberg collected the lab notebooks, and his slide looked like a slide full of moons. Round black-edged circles covered the whole field of view, dozens of them, and not one single onion cell anywhere.

"You've got nothing," said Muhammad, leaning over from the next stool. "What are all those?"

"Cells, I think," Simon said, but even as he said it, his bias toward his own work faded. Real cells had walls and a nucleus and a shape you could label. These were just circles, perfectly round, like coins scattered on glass.

At the counter across the room, Knox was wrestling with the visiting vet's old microscope, the one the clinic kept for school tours. The vet clinic had offered their back room for the science class since the school lab flooded, and the humid little space smelled like dog shampoo. Knox suddenly laughed. "Ha! Mine's all bubbles too. I thought they were cells and I labeled one 'nucleus.'"

"Wait," Simon said. "They're bubbles? Air bubbles?"

"Has to be," Knox said. "Look, I can push one with the corner of the coverslip and it moves."

Simon sat back and stared at his slide. Air. He had dropped the coverslip straight down, flat, like slamming a lid on a jar. If air got trapped under it, it would sit there in round pockets over the cells. The problem wasn't the onion. The problem was how he closed the slide.

He peeled a whisper-thin layer from the inside of his onion piece, laid it on a fresh slide with a drop of water, and picked up a new coverslip. This time he touched one edge to the water first, holding the other side up with tweezers, and lowered it slowly at an angle like a ramp. The drop crawled sideways under the glass, and the slip settled down flat with no circles at all.

Under the microscope, a brick wall of cells appeared, each one neat and rectangular. He could see the darker line of the cell wall, and near the center of one cell, a small round nucleus.

"Muhammad, look," Simon said. "Cell wall, membrane, nucleus. All three."

Muhammad squinted into the eyepiece. "Show me how you lowered that coverslip. I've got two minutes to fix mine."

"Angle it, one edge first," Simon said, already handing him a fresh slip. "It pushes the air out."

Mr. Goldberg's footsteps came down the hall, and Simon picked up his pencil and wrote "nucleus" beside an arrow, grinning.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Elena slid her sketchbook across the dinner table so her mother could see it. "For Auntie Mei's wedding. I found a white dress at the mall, and I thought I'd wear it, since the bride's cousin gets to look fancy too." Her father kept cutting his broccoli, but her grandmother set down her chopsticks so fast that the tips clicked against the bowl.

"Wear white to a wedding?" Her grandmother's voice was quiet, which somehow made it louder. "In my tradition, we wear white to mourn the dead at funerals." The kitchen fan hummed on. Elena felt her cheeks go hot, because she had not known that, and because everyone had stopped eating at once.

"But the bride wears white," Elena said slowly, testing the idea out loud the way she tested answers in math. "The invitations have a white dress code. So it means one thing for Auntie Mei and another thing for Grandmother." She looked from one face to the other. Two people, one color, two completely different pictures in their heads. That was the part she couldn't see directly, and she wanted to check it before she believed it.

"Anika's cousin got married last spring," she went on, "and everyone wore white, and Kenza said her aunt wore white too, at her wedding in France. It's not just one family." Her father nodded. "Different places, different meanings," he said. "Your grandmother wore white when her mother passed. That memory doesn't cease to matter just because we live somewhere else now." Elena had thought picking a dress was simple, and she felt naive now, like she'd solved only half the problem.

"So what do I wear?" she asked. Her grandmother tapped the sketchbook, right on the ribbon Elena had doodled at the waist. "The bride is your aunt. She will wear white, because this wedding follows that way. But you could honor both. Wear something else, something not white, not black either. Red, maybe." She almost smiled. "Red is a good color, where I come from." Elena's instinct was to argue that it was her dress and her choice, but she held it back, because arguing wouldn't tell her what she actually wanted to know.

After dinner she called Anika, then walked two houses down to Kenza's, sketchbook under her arm. The three of them spread colored pencils across Kenza's kitchen table, and Kenza held a red pencil against the white dress drawing. "Better," she said. "Like it means something." Anika leaned over the paper, squinting. "Draw the ribbon gold," she said. "Grandmothers like gold." Elena started coloring in the small bright ribbon, one careful stroke at a time.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, such as a settler's diary, while a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.
story:
The assignment was due Monday, and Logan had left it until Sunday afternoon on purpose, because Grandpa's attic was the best place in the world to leave things until. "Find a primary source," Mr. Nair had said, "and use it to explain why people moved west in the 1800s." Logan had a social studies textbook in his backpack, but Mr. Nair had circled a note on his last worksheet: "Textbook is not enough. Think harder."

The attic smelled like dust and old peppermint. Logan moved a box of tax records, a lamp shaped like a swan, and something furry he decided not to investigate, in case it was about to decompose. Behind a trunk he found a bundle tied with shoelace, and inside it a small book with a cracked leather cover. The handwriting inside was cramped and brown with age. "April the third, 1852. We set out from Illinois. Father says the soil is worn out and the prices here are poor. Six hundred miles to go."

Logan ran downstairs holding the book over his head like a trophy. "Grandpa! Whose is this?"

Grandpa tilted his reading glasses down. "Your great-great-great-grandmother's. She carried that the whole way in a wagon. Careful with the spine, it's older than the state."

Louane, who lived next door and had come over to steal lemonade, peered at the yellowed pages. "Gross, is that a beetle squished in there?"

"That's a pressed flower," Logan said, "and also historical evidence." He was starting to form an idea. The diary was written by a person who actually lived through the trip, right at the time, in 1852. His textbook was written a hundred and fifty years later by somebody studying it. He flipped through his backpack and found the worksheet where Mr. Nair had written it out plain as a road sign: a primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, like a settler's diary, and a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.

"So this diary is my primary source," Logan said, "and the textbook is secondary. Which means my report can say why her family moved, in her own words. Worn-out soil. Bad prices."

Louane frowned. "Couldn't you just get that from the textbook?"

"The textbook wasn't in the wagon, Louane. This book was. It ate the same dust."

Jonas arrived just then, because Sunday afternoons at Grandpa's worked like a magnet that way. He read a page aloud in a deep explorer voice, then held the diary up beside the textbook. "Look, they're parallel. Diary, textbook. Same story, one's the original and one's the copycat."

"Sort of," Logan said. He noticed something odd, though. In the margin of one page, great-great-great-grandmother had drawn a little horseshoe, then drawn it again flipped, like a mirror. Two horseshoes, perfectly matched. "She made symmetry out of a horseshoe. She must have been bored."

"She was in a wagon for six hundred miles," Jonas said. "I'd draw horseshoes too."

Logan spread his report paper across the kitchen table and wrote the first line: "My primary source is a settler's diary from 1852." Grandpa slid the lemonade over, and Louane read the horseshoe page upside down, and outside a real horse clopped by on the road, which made all three of them look up at once.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Masking fluid is a liquid rubber painted onto areas to keep them white; once it dries you paint over it, then rub it off to reveal the paper.
story:
Mr. Mori set the small jar on the table between them and said only, "For the highlights, if you want them." Jacob stared at it. The jar held a pale, gloopy liquid that looked like glue, and he could not imagine what glue had to do with painting a portrait of his grandmother in her beaded necklace.

His first attempt that Monday had been a disaster. He had tried to paint around each tiny bead to leave it white, and his brush had thwarted him at every turn, blooming dark pigment into the little white dots until the necklace looked like a smudge of gravel. Troy had leaned over from the next table and winced. "Those were supposed to be sparkly, right?"

"Everything's supposed to be a lot of things," Jacob muttered. The problem, he decided, was one he could not see directly: the white of the paper itself. To keep a bead white he had to keep paint off it, but the paint went wherever the water went, and water crept. He needed something invisible that worked while he was not looking, like a fence built before the flood.

So on Wednesday he tested an idea. He dipped a cheap brush into the mystery jar and dabbed the liquid onto the beads in his sketch, one small blob per bead. Viktor watched from across the table. "That's masking fluid," he said. "You let it dry, paint right over it, then rub it off and the paper underneath is still white." Jacob's frugal instinct made him wince at wasting any on a test, but he painted a stripe of it on scrap paper too, so he could check when it was dry without poking the real thing.

When the blobs had set, he mixed a strong dark wash for the shirt and swept it straight across the whole necklace. His hand shook a little, because it felt like ruining everything on purpose. The dark dried. Then he took a clean eraser and rubbed. A bead emerged, pure white, bright as a tooth. He rubbed again and another appeared, then a dozen more, scattered like stars in the dark cloth. He grinned so hard his cheeks hurt.

"Look," he said, and turned the paper toward Troy and Viktor. Troy put out his fist, and Jacob bumped it without looking, already reaching for the frugal little jar to dab masking fluid onto the highlight in his grandmother's eyes.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: Bonds from borrowers more likely to fail to pay are called high-yield or 'junk' bonds, and they must pay higher interest to attract lenders.
story:
Gabriel sat in the back of Mr. Dela Cruz's classroom with a printed page of pretend investments in front of him. The assignment was to pick one stock and one bond, then explain which was riskier and why. Ludovic leaned over from the next desk and tapped the bond column. "Look at this one. Eight percent. The others are all around four."

Gabriel studied the numbers. Twice the interest. That seemed like free money, and free money always made him suspicious. He remembered his uncle's fishing vessel, the one that sat rusting at the dock because nobody would insure it; people charged more to take on trouble. He wondered if lending worked the same way.

"So what's the catch?" Josue asked, sliding his chair around. "Maybe there isn't one. Maybe it's just a better deal."

"Then everybody would buy it," Gabriel said. "And the price would go up until it wasn't a better deal anymore." He copied the borrower's name onto a scrap of paper and looked it up on the classroom computer. The company had missed payments before. Missed payments twice, in fact, in the last few years. He felt something click into place, like a key finding its lock.

Mr. Dela Cruz wandered past and glanced at Gabriel's screen but said nothing, which Gabriel took as a small encouragement. He turned back to Ludovic and Josue. "I think I've got it," he said. "When a bond pays way more interest, it's because the borrower is more likely to not pay you back at all. The higher interest is the bait. There's even a name for them. They're called high-yield bonds, or junk bonds. They have to pay more to get anyone to lend."

"Junk," Josue repeated, grinning. "So the catch is built into the name."

"Exactly." Gabriel wrote his answer out in careful sentences. The stock could drop in value, he argued, but you still owned a piece of the company. The junk bond promised you a fixed payment from a borrower who might fail to give it, and if that happened, you were not immune to loss just because it was called a bond. Bonds could be riskier than stocks. It depended on who was borrowing.

When Mr. Dela Cruz collected the papers, he read Gabriel's page standing in the aisle, then gave a slow nod. "I have to confess," he said quietly, "most students pick the eight percent bond without asking why." Gabriel looked down at his scrap of paper, the borrower's name circled twice, and folded it into his pocket.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading the dough makes the gluten stronger and stretchier.
story:
Grace had promised her mother a fresh loaf of bread before dinner, and the kitchen extension cord wasn't long enough, so she'd carried the stand mixer, flour, and a bag of yeast out to the backyard picnic table. The tenant in the basement apartment, Mr. Carvalho, was watering the tomato plants by the fence, and the smell of the warm June afternoon mixed with the dust rising off the flour sack.

The first dough she mixed turned out wrong. It tore when she pulled at it, like wet paper instead of something alive, and she hadn't even started kneading yet. She was about to dump it in the compost when Carmen arrived, carrying the notes Grace had missed from the cooking elective she'd enrolled in back in September. "Leila said you were baking out here," Carmen said, dropping onto the bench. "Also, rain's imminent. Look at that sky."

Grace looked at the sky, then back at her torn dough. "I don't get it. Last week my dough got stretchy and I could see through it when I pulled it thin. This one just breaks." Carmen flipped through the notes, but Grace stopped her. "No, wait. Let me think." Last week she had used water and flour from the same bag. Today she'd used milk instead of water, because her mother liked milk bread. She pushed the milk carton aside and started a new dough with water only, watching how the flour soaked it up.

They took turns kneading at the picnic table while fat clouds piled up over the neighbor's roof. After a few minutes the dough changed under Grace's hands, turning smooth and springy, and she stretched a piece until it glowed thin without tearing. "There it is," she said. "Gluten. It forms when the proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading makes it stronger and stretchier." Carmen frowned. "So milk doesn't count as water?" "It counts for flavor," Grace said, "but it didn't give me what I needed today."

Her mother came out with a dish towel over her shoulder just as the first drops hit the tomato plants. Grace carried the dough inside in the bowl, and while it rose on the counter she printed a new page for her recipe binder: water, not milk, ten full minutes of kneading, then patience. When the loaf finally came out of the oven that evening, golden and crackling, Mr. Carvalho knocked at the back door, still holding his watering can. "That smell reached the basement," he said. Grace cut him the first warm slice, and the steam curled up between them.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
story:
Ariana sat in the waiting room of Dr. Patel's office with her right wrist wrapped in a soft brace, wishing she had not tried to mimic the move she saw in a skate video last weekend. On the chair beside her, Ray flipped through a pile of worn magazines and held one up. "Look at this. It says kids who eat fish three times a week get better grades. We should tell your mom to buy fish."

Ariana took the magazine and read the headline twice. Something about it bothered her, the way a loose thread bothers you before you can name it. "My grandmother ate fish almost every day," she said slowly, "and she left school at ten. So it can't just be the fish." Ray shrugged. "Maybe your grandmother is the one exception."

While they waited, Ariana borrowed a pen from the front desk and started a list on the back of a crossword page. Kids who eat lots of fish: maybe they live near the coast, maybe their families have more money for fresh food, maybe their parents have time to cook real dinners instead of grabbing fast food on the way to work. Ray leaned over. "So the fish and the good grades could both come from something else?" Ariana tapped the pen. "Like how ice cream sales and sunburns both go up together in summer. The ice cream doesn't cause the sunburn. Hot weather causes both." Ray grinned. "You just broke that headline."

Mr. Jean-Louis, the school librarian, was in the next chair waiting for his own appointment, and he had been listening with his coat still buttoned. He caught Ariana's eye. "My daughter did a science project on that," he said. "Correlation does not prove causation." Ariana wrote the words down carefully, sounding them out, and Ray copied them into his phone. "That's going in my next current events report," Ray said. "Mr. Jean-Louis, you can be my source." The librarian laughed and said he would accept the honor, though he warned them his knees made him a more reliable source on weather than on fish.

When the nurse finally called her name, Ariana stood up and noticed an older man by the window struggling to reach a water fountain with his cane in one hand. She got there first, filled a small paper cup, and handed it to him. "Thank you, young lady," he said. "You're a resilient one, that brace and all." Ariana smiled. "It's just a sprain. And thanks to this," she said, lifting the magazine page with her good hand, "I'm going to eat my fish and do my homework anyway, just in case." The man raised his cup to her like a toast.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place.
story:
The old diary lay open on the library table, its cracked spine held together with yellowed tape. Autumn turned the page carefully, the way Mr. Mensah had shown her, and read the faded ink aloud. "April the third, 1846. Papa says the bank will take the farm in Missouri if we cannot pay, and there is land in Oregon a man may claim for nothing. Mama wept, but she has stopped arguing."

"So why did they go?" Hillary asked, chewing her pencil.

Autumn read it again. It was like there were two different engines pulling the family in the same direction. "The bank thing is pushing them out of Missouri," she said slowly. "And the free land is pulling them toward Oregon." She wrote PUSH and PULL at the top of her notes. "Mr. Mensah called those push factors and pull factors. Push factors drive people away from home, and pull factors attract them to a new place."

"Then it's easy," Hillary said, and began listing. Bank trouble, push. Free land, pull. Mama's brother already in Oregon, pull. Then Autumn reached a line that stopped her: "The wheat has failed three years running, and I fear our Lucy will not thrive here." She stared at it. She had put the wheat under push, because it was bad news. But was failing wheat really driving them out, or was it just one more reason the farm could not support them?
