She tested her idea out loud. "What if the wheat isn't a push factor at all? The bank taking the farm is the push. The wheat is why the push works. Without the debt, they'd stay and try again." Hillary frowned, then tapped the line about Lucy. "Sickly child. That's a push too, isn't it? Or is it that Oregon's clean air is a pull?" They argued for ten minutes, crossing out and rewriting, until the notebook looked like a battlefield.

Then Autumn found something tucked between the last pages: a small folded letter, unsigned, in the same handwriting but lighter, as if written later. "We have been in the Willamette Valley one year. The claim is ours. Lucy is fat and brown and loud. Mama has begun to plant flowers." Hillary leaned over her shoulder, and for a moment neither of them said anything. Every push and pull on their list had come true, in reverse. Autumn copied the letter word for word onto a fresh page and underlined the last line twice. "This is the fundamental thing we were missing," she said. "The diary tells us why they left. This tells us what happened next." Hillary grinned and slid the notebook toward her. "Read it to me again," she said. "Start from the part about Mama."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
Alicia found the paintbrush in the garage two weeks after Grandpa died, wedged behind a bucket where he must have hidden it from himself. The bristles were stiff with dried blue paint, because he had been reckless about rinsing his tools, and the handle still smelled faintly of turpentine. She carried it to the kitchen table, where her mother was folding paper into small ingot shapes, folding and turning, folding and turning, until each one looked like a little gold boat.

"Why are you making those?" Alicia asked.

"For Qingming," her mother said. "It's usually April fourth or fifth, this year the fifth. Families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings." She set a finished ingot beside the others, twelve of them in a row like a tiny fleet. "Your cousin Mei is coming with us."

Alicia turned the paintbrush over in her hands. She had a theory, or maybe it was only a wish, that Grandpa could still notice things, and she wanted to test it before she let herself believe it. She hypothesized that if he could notice anything, he would notice his own brush. So she slipped it into the offering bag with the paper ingots, some oranges, and a bag of the licorice he used to eat while he worked. If the idea was wrong, nothing would happen and she would only feel a little foolish. If it was right, well, she would know something no one could prove to her.

On the fifth of April they drove out to the cemetery with Mei and her parents. The gravestone had gathered a winter of grit and birdseed, because a sparrow is a scavenger and someone kept feeding the birds from the bench nearby. Mei swept the stone with a small whisk broom while Alicia wiped the carved letters of his name with a damp cloth, one stroke at a time, the way he had taught her to clean a paintbrush even though he never did it himself. Her mother set out the oranges and the paper ingots, and the licorice, and Alicia placed the paintbrush last, handle facing the stone so it would be easy to pick up.

Mei leaned close and whispered, "Do you think he minds that it's dirty?"

"He left it dirty," Alicia whispered back. "That's how he'd want it."

The wind moved through the grass, and the licorice bag rustled against the stone like something shifting its weight.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Eid al-Fitr is the Muslim celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month in which many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset.
story:
Isabella climbed the porch steps behind Zaiden, holding a plate of her mother's cinnamon buns like it was evidence in a trial. She had spent the whole morning on a mock trial team, arguing that the defendant in their practice case was innocent, and her brain was still stuck in lawyer mode. So when Zaiden's grandmother opened the door already laughing, and the whole house smelled like cardamom and fried dough, Isabella noticed something that didn't fit. It was barely ten in the morning, and the table was loaded with food as if it were a feast at sunset.

"Who eats this much this early?" she whispered to Zaiden.

"Everybody, today," he said. "It's Eid al-Fitr. That's the celebration marking the end of Ramadan."

"Ramadan," Isabella repeated. She filed the word away the way she'd file a clue. Zaiden's aunt called everyone to the table, and plates started moving fast, and Isabella watched Zaiden's father take the first bite of something sweet with his eyes closed, like it mattered more than usual.

She turned the puzzle over while she ate. For a month, she was pretty sure, Zaiden had turned down lunch at school every single day, even pizza day, even when Abel offered him half a sandwich. She had assumed he wasn't hungry. Now she tested a different idea: if Ramadan meant going without food from dawn until sunset, then a whole month of that would end with a celebration where eating in the morning was the whole point. That would explain the giant breakfast. It would also explain why Zaiden's little cousin was stacking cookies like they were treasure.

"You figured it out," Zaiden said, watching her face. "You've got your courtroom look."

"Guilty of fasting all month," Isabella said. "I simulated it yesterday, you know. Skipped breakfast and lunch to see what it was like. I made it to two o'clock and then ate an entire bag of crackers." She winced. "A whole month. From dawn until sunset."

Zaiden laughed so hard his cousin looked over. "You tried it? That's actually kind of great."

His grandmother pressed a warm pastry into Isabella's hands and said something to Zaiden in Urdu, smiling.

"She says you're an honourary family member now," he translated. "Also that you should stand back from the candles on the side table, because the decorations are flammable."

Isabella moved her sleeve away from the flickering flame, took a bite, and decided the pastry was the best evidence she'd gathered all day.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: Outlining first separates planning from sentence-writing, so a writer decides what to say before worrying about how to word it.
story:
Ethan had been staring at the same blank page for eleven minutes. Mr. Cruz's assignment was on the board: take a position on whether the school should keep vending machines, and support it with three points. Around him, pencils were already scratching. Beside him, Ryann was writing so fast her hand looked like it might catch fire, because she wanted the fastest finished draft in the class, and she wanted everyone to know it.

Ethan had ideas. He had too many ideas, actually, and every time he tried to write the first sentence, he'd think of a better point and cross everything out. He was becoming a chronic starter. Page one, line one, over and over. Was there something wrong with the way he was attacking this? He watched Ryann zoom ahead and wondered if speed was really the whole game, or if she was just building a house with no blueprint.

Then he noticed Reese. Reese hadn't written a sentence either. Instead he'd drawn three short lines on his paper, like a shopping list. When Ethan leaned over, he saw it: keep machines, then three quick phrases after it. Money for clubs. Students stay after school. Better choices added this year.

"You're not writing the essay?" Ethan whispered.

"First I'm writing what I'm going to say," Reese said. "Planning and sentence-writing are different jobs. If I plan first, I decide what to say before I worry about how to word it."

Ethan tried it. He set his essay voice aside and just listed: ban the machines, then three reasons in plain little bullets. It took two minutes. No sentences, no fancy words, nothing to cross out. When he looked at the three bullets sitting there, he could suddenly see which one was strongest, which one was weakest, and which order made the argument climb instead of slump. The list was like an x-ray of his own thinking.

Then he drafted, and it was strange how the sentences came easier. His stamina held out, too, because half the work was already done. Ryann finished first and raised her hand triumphantly, but when Mr. Cruz walked the rows, he stopped at her desk for a long moment. Her opening sentence was gorgeous, but her third paragraph was arguing the opposite of her first.

"Ethan," Mr. Cruz said next, tapping Ethan's bullet list at the top of the page. "This is what I want to see more of. From now on, I'm going to enforce this. Outline before drafting, everyone."

Ryann looked at Ethan's paper, then at her own tangled draft, and groaned.

"So," she said, "are you going to show me how you did that, or what?"

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
story:
Xavier spread three paper airplanes across the workbench in his grandfather's garage, next to the old generator that hadn't run since last summer. His hypothesis, though he didn't use that word yet, was simple: a plane with wider wings would glide farther than one with narrow wings. He had folded the planes from identical sheets of paper, and he planned to measure every flight with the tape measure hanging on the wall.

Robin arrived on her bike, helmet still clipped under her chin. "Which one do you think wins?" she asked, picking up the wide-winged plane and holding it up to the bare bulb that hung from the ceiling.

"The wide one. It catches more air," Xavier said. "That's my hypothesis. A testable guess. Ms. Eze says that's what a hypothesis is, and the whole point is that an experiment can prove you wrong."

They started in the garage. Xavier threw each plane from the same chalk line on the concrete floor, counted to make sure the timing matched, and wrote down the distances. The wide plane flew about six meters. Then Robin had an idea. "Let's see how far they go outside. There's more room on the driveway."

Outside, the wide plane sailed past the end of the tape measure, and the narrow one tumbled sideways and landed in the hedge. Xavier wrote the numbers down, then stopped, pencil hovering. Something felt wrong. He looked at the flag on the neighbor's mailbox, snapping and trembling in the breeze.

"Wait," he said. "This doesn't count. In the garage there was no wind. Out here the wind is pushing them. The wind changed, so we're not really testing the wings anymore. We're testing the weather." He thought for a moment, tapping the pencil against his knee. "For a fair test, everything except the thing we're testing has to stay the same. Same amount of paper, same throwing spot, same timing. Even the temperature should match, or at least be close. If we throw one plane indoors and the other outside in the wind, we can't trust the answer."

"So what do we do?" Robin asked.

"We do the whole thing in the garage, both planes, same throws, same everything. Then the only difference is the wings." He scooped up the planes and carried them back inside, past the generator and the smell of machine oil, and rechalked the line on the floor. Ms. Eze, who was watering her garden next door, waved through the open door.

They threw again. Xavier anticipated that the wide plane would win by a lot, and it did win, but only by about half a meter, close enough that he wrote an approximate distance rather than pretending he'd measured it exactly. He ran the test twice more. Wide, wide, wide, every single time.

Robin looked at the clipboard, then at the two planes lying side by side on the bench. "So your guess was right. But it was right for the small version of right."

Xavier grinned and picked up a fresh sheet of paper. "Now we test narrow wings folded from two sheets taped together."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
story:
Connor stood in the produce section holding his mother's shopping list and a twenty-dollar bill. Tonight he was making potato soup for the whole family, because his mother had pulled a double shift and his father was driving his sister home from practice. He had promised a competent dinner, not just toast, and soup seemed safe. He picked out potatoes, carrots, celery, and then stopped at the onions.

"Cooking for the whole family?" said Dyson, who was stacking his own basket with cereal for his own mother. "My mom says she'd advocate for takeout every night if my dad let her. What are you making?"

"Potato soup. It's my first real dinner."

"You're going to cry," Dyson said.

"Why?"

"Onions. My brother says you can't chop one without your eyes streaming." Dyson leaned on the cart. "Wear swim goggles. That's what he does."

Connor paid for the groceries and carried the bags the four blocks home. Ms. Moretti was watering her window boxes as he passed, and she waved him in to borrow her big soup pot, which he promised to return washed.

In the kitchen he peeled the potatoes and carrots without trouble. Then he set the onion on the cutting board, sliced into it, and within seconds his eyes were burning and his face was wet. He wiped his cheeks with his sleeve and kept chopping, blinking hard, and by the time the onion was in the pot his vision was blurry. He ran the tap and splashed water on his face.

He sat down and thought about it. He had not been sad, and the onion had not touched his eyes at all. So something had to travel from the onion to his face. He looked up a video on his mother's tablet, and the person on it said the line he needed: "Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches your eyes and makes them water." Enzymes. The word stuck. He paused the video and wrote it on the back of the list, then underlined it. The gas had to float upward from the cut surface. That was a rule he could test.

He put the second onion in the freezer for ten minutes, then brought it back to the board. He cut it slowly with his head turned as far from the board as he could manage, and he noticed the difference right away. His eyes stung a little, but nothing like before. Cold and distance both seemed to help, though he could not say which one mattered more. That would take more onions than he had.

The soup simmered, and he tasted it, added salt, tasted again. When his mother came home at eight, the kitchen smelled like a real dinner. She looked at the cutting board and the tissue box he had moved next to it.

"What's the tissue box for?" she asked.

"Science," Connor said, and ladled her a bowl.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Herman Snellen developed his eye chart of rows of shrinking letters in 1862.
story:
Lily stood in front of the optical shop at the mall and read the eye chart on the wall for the third time. The top letter, a big black E, was easy. The row below it was a blur she could only guess at, which was exactly why she was here. The school nurse had made her guess at a chart just like it two weeks ago, and she had gotten the small rows badly wrong.

"You're going to look like a rodent in those tiny frames," Aarav said, pointing at a display case. "A really smart rodent."

"You ridicule me one more time and I'm telling Mr. Qureshi you skipped his homework club to come here." Lily said it without turning around, because she was still staring at the chart. Something about it bothered her. Every chart she had ever seen, at school, at the nurse's office, and now here, had the same shrinking rows of letters, and the same letters in the same order. She had assumed the nurse had picked some random page from a book. But a random page wouldn't match a chart in a mall in a different town.

"Miss Ahmed will see you now," the receptionist said.

Mr. Qureshi, the optometrist, turned out to be the same man who ran the hardware store near school, which Lily found bizarre until she remembered he had mentioned once that his brother owned this shop. He sat her in a chair, flipped a lens machine in front of her face, and pointed at a projected chart on the far wall.

"Read the smallest line you can," he said.

She got to the fourth row and stopped. "Before we do this, can I ask something? Is every chart in the world the same? Because the nurse's chart had these exact letters, and yours does too."

Mr. Qureshi grinned. "You noticed that, did you? It's called a Snellen chart. Herman Snellen developed it in 1862, rows of shrinking letters. That nurse's chart you saw is older than anyone's great-grandparents."

Lily did the math in her head. If the chart was from 1862, then everyone who had ever squinted at those same shrinking rows, for over a hundred and fifty years, had read the same letters she just failed to read. "So when the nurse said I failed, she compared me to everyone since 1862?"

"More or less," Mr. Qureshi said. He spun the lenses. "Now, one or two?"

"Two," Lily said, and the fourth row snapped into focus so sharply she laughed out loud.

She wanted to test one more thing before she trusted the numbers. "If the chart is that old, could my eyes just be shaped like everyone's back then? Maybe it's not me, it's the chart." She knew it was a weak idea even as she said it.

Mr. Qureshi shook his head. "The chart is old. Your eyeballs are eleven. Read me the last row."

She read it, every letter, down to the tiny F at the bottom.

At the display case, Lily picked black frames with round lenses, the biggest ones on the shelf. "Rodent," Aarav said. "Giant genius rodent." She put them on, and the food court sign across the mall hallway was sharp enough to read, all the way down to the small print about refills.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
story:
Amelia had forty dollars and one weekend, and the sneakers she wanted cost ninety. She stood in the shoe store window at Riverside Mall, staring at a poster of the runner Darius Cole lunging across a finish line. Above him, enormous letters read "EVERYONE WHO'S ANYONE IS RUNNING IN VOLT-9S." Below that, in smaller type, came the words "revolutionary" and "unstoppable." Behind her, Lexi tugged her sleeve. "Darius Cole wears them," Lexi said, as if that settled everything. "If they're good enough for the fastest guy alive, they're good enough for us." Amelia felt the pull of it, the way the poster seemed to be full of people she couldn't see, all of them already running in Volt-9s while she stood still in her old shoes. She had almost decided to empty her savings when she remembered Monday.

Monday was the deadline. Ms. Rowe's history project, a research paper on wartime posters, was due first period, and Amelia had barely started. She'd been putting it off for two weeks, and now the library was closed until Sunday afternoon, which gave her one day to finish. "Come on," she told Lexi, "I have to at least look at the poster exhibits in the bookstore."

In the mall bookstore, between a display of cookbooks and a rack of magazines, she found a whole shelf on World War II. She pulled down a thick book with a poster on the cover of a stern man pointing his finger, and flipped through it until she found a chapter called "Who Taught People to See Through This?" She read a page standing up, one finger holding her place. The Institute for Propaganda Analysis had been founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda. Ordinary people, back then, learning to spot tricks. She said the name out loud by accident. "Institute for Propaganda Analysis," she murmured.

"That sounds like a spy thing," said Alexander, who had appeared beside her holding a book about the human body. He opened it to a diagram. "Check this out, an intestine is like seven meters long." Amelia glanced over, then went back to her book. The institute, she read, had made lists of common tricks, and she recognized them one by one: get on the bandwagon, loaded words, celebrity endorsement. Her stomach did something strange. The Volt-9 poster had done all three at once.

Then her phone buzzed. A message from Lexi, sent from two stores away: "Come back. They just announced Volt-9s are almost SOLD OUT and the sale ends at 9 tonight. This is our only chance!!" Amelia read it twice. Almost sold out. Only chance. She typed back: "That's a deadline trick. They want us to panic and buy before we think. I'm staying here. Bring Alexander's book money and meet me." Lexi replied with a single frowning face, then, a minute later: "Fine. But if they're gone, it's your fault."

When Lexi and Alexander arrived, Amelia spread three scratch papers on the bookstore floor and made a systematic list: what the ad claimed, what evidence it gave, and what it actually wanted her to feel. "Darius Cole probably got paid," she said. "Everyone who's anyone isn't everyone. And revolutionary is just a loaded word for a shoe." Alexander grinned. "So your plan is to intervene between Lexi and the cash register?" "My plan," Amelia said, "is to finish this paper, save my money, and buy last year's model, which is probably the same shoe in a quieter color." Lexi sat down heavily beside them, looked at the poster of the pointing man in Amelia's book, then at her phone full of exclamation points, and slid the phone into her pocket. "Okay," she said. "Teach me the list."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
story:
At dinner, Brielle set her phone face-up beside her plate so she could watch for Mckenzie's reply. The science fair was in three weeks, and their project had just fallen apart.

"Dad," she said, poking her pasta, "remember that study Mr. Bouchard told us about? The one where they tested a new medicine on people who were really tired all the time?"

Her dad sprinkled cheese on his plate. "The one from the news article, right. The one you said was a big deal."

"Because hundreds of people took it and got better. That's evidence. Not like the video Elliot found, where one guy says a smoothie cured his tiredness in a week." She stabbed a meatball. "One guy. One week. That's a story, not a study. But here's the problem. Mckenzie wants us to copy the smoothie recipe and test it on ourselves for the fair, and I keep texting her why that won't work and she keeps texting back, so?"

The phone buzzed. Brielle read it aloud: "just let people pick which one they want to try."

"That sounds fair," her dad said. "People like choices."

Brielle stopped chewing. Something about that sentence snagged in her head like a sleeve on a nail. If people picked, who would pick the smoothie? Probably the people who already believed in it. And who would pick the medicine? Different people, maybe older people, maybe sicker people. The two groups wouldn't be the same before the test even started. Her eyes went wide.

"Dad. That's it. That's the flaw. If people choose, the groups aren't the same. In the real study, the scientists didn't let anybody pick. They assigned people to groups at random, like a lottery, so that differences like age or health would be spread evenly between the groups." She was talking fast now. "So if more people in one group got better, it couldn't just be because they were younger to start with. It had to be the medicine."

"So how will you test your smoothie?" her dad asked, smiling.

"Random assignment. I'll put everybody's name in a jar. Half pull a green slip, half pull a blue. Green gets the smoothie, blue gets plain juice that looks the same." She grabbed her phone and typed while her dad cleared his plate. The tablet in the kitchen dissolved into sleep mode, unused all evening, which in their house meant serious thinking had happened.

Mckenzie's reply came as her dad was scraping leftovers into a container: "ooo like a defendant can't pick their own jury. ok fine. jar idea is actually good."

Brielle laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her milk. Then she wrote back one line: "Bring the jar Monday. Elliot draws first."

Her dad shook his head, smiling, and slid the last meatball onto her plate. "For the scientist," he said.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Colton had one thing on his mind when he climbed onto the school bus, and it was not the math quiz. It was his birthday party. He wanted to invite the whole class, all twenty-six of them, and his mom had said he could send the invitation by email if he did it himself.

He slid into the seat behind Bradley, who was already peering at Colton's phone over the seatback. "You're inviting everybody?" Bradley asked. "Even people you barely talk to?"

"Everybody," Colton said. "It's the whole class or nobody. That's the rule I made up."

Charles-Olivier turned around from the row across the aisle, headphones hanging around his neck. "Wait. If you put the whole class in the To line, everyone sees everyone's address. My sister did that for her swim team and it turned into a disaster. Somebody replied to all, and then everybody replied to all, and it filled up my dad's inbox for a week."

Colton looked down at the email draft on his screen. Twenty-six addresses, stacked like bricks in the To field. He assessed the situation. Charles-Olivier was probably right, and "probably right" was good enough when your dad's inbox was on the line. But how could you send one email to twenty-six people without twenty-six people seeing each other?

His thumb hovered over the screen. Then he noticed it, tucked below the To line: a small gray link that read Add BCC. He had never tapped it before. He tapped it now, and a second empty field appeared, quiet as a second pocket.

"What's BCC?" he asked.

"Blind carbon copy," Charles-Olivier said. "People you put there get the message, but the others can't see their addresses."

Colton tested it before he trusted it. He sent a practice message to himself, his own address in BCC, with only Bradley in the To line. When it arrived, he checked what he could see. There was Bradley, and nothing else. His own address, the one hidden in that second field, was invisible, gone as if he had never been on the list at all.

"It works," he said. He cut all twenty-six addresses from the To line and pasted them into BCC. In the To field, the one everyone would see, he typed his own address, alone.

Bradley made a pivot on his knees so he faced backward fully, resting his chin on the seatback. "So everyone gets the invite, and nobody gets spammed."

"Robust plan," Colton said, and pressed send. The bus swayed around the corner by the hardware store, and somewhere out there, twenty-six inboxes began to fill.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Raw onion tastes sharp, but cooking it slowly over low heat makes it soft and sweet as its natural sugars turn golden brown.
story:
Matteo held the knife the way the video had shown him, curled fingertips tucked under like a claw, knuckles riding the blade. His dad had agreed to postpone dinner until seven so Matteo could make the sauce himself, start to finish.

"Okay," his dad said, setting a cutting board on the counter. "Onions first. Low heat, and patience."

Gordon had come over to help, or mostly to watch. He stood at the doorway with the wary look of a kid approaching a siege. "I don't do onions," he announced. "Raw onion is disgusting. It's like eating a burn."

"You're not eating it raw," Matteo said. He cut the onion in half, peeled it, and started chopping, claw grip steady, the knife tip never leaving the board. His eyes streamed, and he laughed through it. Gordon slid him a paper towel without being asked, which Matteo accepted gratefully.

The pieces went into a wide pan with a slick of oil, over the smallest flame the stove would hold. Matteo wanted to turn it up, because nothing seemed to be happening, but he remembered what the recipe card said: slow. So he waited, stirring now and then, while the onions sat there looking pale and lazy, almost dormant, for what felt like ages.

Then they began to change. The edges went soft, then gold, then a deeper amber, and the kitchen filled with a smell that made even Gordon drift closer to the stove.

"That's the same onion?" Gordon asked, peering into the pan. "The sharp one?"

"Raw onion tastes sharp," Matteo said, stirring, "but if you cook it slowly over low heat, it gets soft and sweet. Its natural sugars turn golden brown." He lifted a sliver out with the spoon, blew on it, and held it out. "Try."

Gordon changed his mind right at the last second, leaning forward instead of back. He took the piece, chewed, and his eyebrows went up. "Okay. That's good. Can I have more of those?"

"Later. First it goes in the sauce." Matteo crushed the canned tomatoes with his hands, sloshing them in with the golden onions, and let everything simmer while he boiled the pasta. Gordon, who had sworn off onions since kindergarten, stationed himself by the stove and kept sneaking sweet amber slivers from the pan until Matteo finally tipped the rest straight into the pot.

They set the table together, forks and folded napkins, and called Matteo's dad down. At dinner, Gordon went back for seconds, then pushed his bowl across for a third helping of sauce.

"Tell my mom the slow way," he said, mouth half full. "The very slow way. The slowest way there is."

Matteo grinned and ladled it on.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Robert Hooke named cells in his 1665 book Micrographia after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope.
story:
Harrison had one sheet of paper and forty minutes before the bus left, and the paper had three blank lines waiting for labels: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. The microscope at the museum's specimen station smelled like dust and hand sanitizer. He clipped the prepared slide of onion skin under the clips, the way Mr. Sánchez had shown their class at school, and bent down to look. Nothing. Just gray.

"You have to adjust the fine focus," said Eshal, who had already finished her own drawing and was now leaning over a glass case on the far wall. "Little knob, not the big one. The big one just makes everything worse."

Harrison turned the small knob a hair at a time, and the gray swam, sharpened, and broke into shapes. Rows of brick-like compartments, each with a dark dot near its edge and a darker line around its outside. He started his drawing, mapping the outer wall first, then trying to decide whether the faint inner line was the membrane or just the wall being thick on one side. That was the part he kept getting wrong in class, and he was getting it wrong again now.

"Come look at this," Eshal called. "There's a copy of a drawing from some old book. It looks exactly like your slide."

Harrison left the microscope and read the card beside the yellowed page. The drawing showed tiny boxy compartments in a slice of cork, drawn by a man named Robert Hooke. "That's what mine looks like under the scope," he said. "Same boxes."

"He called them cells," Eshal read off the card. "In his book. Micrographia, 1665."

Harrison stared at the drawing, then back across the room at his microscope. Cork came from tree bark, he thought, and onion skin from a plant too, so maybe the boxes weren't a coincidence. Maybe every living thing had them, and people had only noticed once someone stuck something thin enough under a lens. His problem with the labels suddenly felt smaller. If Hooke could figure out the boxes, Harrison could figure out the lines. He went back and adjusted the focus again, slower this time, and the faint inner line appeared clearly inside the wall, hugging it. Membrane. The dark dot had to be the nucleus. He wrote all three labels and held the sheet up.

On the way to the bus, they passed a display case with a lump of glass shaped like a frozen splash, a card explaining it had been molten when the artist poured it. Jakub was waiting at the door, waving them on. "Did you finish your labels?" he asked.

"All three," Harrison said, "and I know why the boxes are called cells, too."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
story:
Victoria crouched beside the lettuce bed in Ms. Sandhu's garden and counted the ragged holes again. Eleven leaves had been nibbled since Tuesday, always at night, always close to the ground. She wanted to win the young gardeners' prize at the harvest fair, and she needed her lettuce whole, but something unseen was dismantling her chances bite by bite.

"It's rabbits," said Deegan, leaning on the fence. "Has to be. Rabbits eat everything." Ayan shook his head. "Rabbits would eat the middle of the leaf. These edges are too tidy. I say slugs." Victoria frowned. They could argue until the sun went down behind the parliament of owls that roosted in Ms. Sandhu's old oak, and they would still be guessing. A guess was only worth something if you could check it. She remembered a battered book she had found on Ms. Sandhu's porch shelf, about a philosopher named Karl Popper, who argued in a book first published in 1934 that an idea was scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong. Her rabbit idea would pass that test. Slugs would too. The plan came to her all at once.

"If rabbits are doing this," she said, "they'll leave footprints. So I'll spread flour around the bed tonight. If we find no rabbit tracks, and the leaves are still eaten, then rabbits are innocent." Deegan looked stung. "You're setting it up to fail?" "I'm setting it up so we can find out," Victoria said. She sifted a ring of white flour over the dark soil, fine as snow, and marked the last nibbled leaf with a twist tie.

Morning arrived cool and gray. Victoria tiptoed out with Ayan and Deegan at seven, before anyone's shoes could spoil the flour. The ring was there, the flour ruffled by dew, and across it ran a scatter of tiny three-toed prints, delicate as stitching, hopping from leaf to leaf. Birds. The three of them stared. "Rabbits cleared," Ayan said quietly. Even the slug idea had fallen apart, since the marks began and ended on top of the leaves, not underneath where slugs crawl. But birds did not usually eat lettuce at night, and that part still bothered her, so at dawn the next day Victoria sat perfectly still on the porch step with a thermos of tea and watched.

Just as the sky turned pink, sparrows dropped from the oak, quick and agile, and worked the lettuce edges like little gardeners pruning. Ms. Sandhu came out with her watering can, watched them too, and laughed. "Cheeky things. They want the moisture on a dry morning." Victoria fetched an old net from the shed and stretched it over the bed on bent coat hangers, and by Friday every new leaf had come through whole. At the harvest fair, when the judge asked how she had tracked down her culprit, Victoria said, "I spread flour for footprints, because if no rabbit tracks showed up, my rabbit idea was wrong and I'd have to let it go." The judge smiled. "Then what would have proved your bird idea wrong?" Victoria thought for a moment. "No bird prints at all, and the net stopping nothing." The judge wrote something on her clipboard, and out on the green, Deegan was waving her over to the ribbon table.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Health agencies recommend scrubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, including after changing a diaper and before preparing food.
story:
Muhammad tapped the message into the family group chat as soon as the neighbor's door clicked shut behind him: "Babysitting gig STARTED. Baby Maya is asleep. Easy money." His mom replied with three party emojis, and his cousin sent, "Famous last words." He grinned and pocketed the phone. Then, from the nursery, a smell drifted out that was not easy, not asleep, and definitely not money.

The diaper change was a battle. Baby Maya wiggled like a fish, grabbed her own sock, and laughed at Muhammad's grimace. He drafted a new strategy: hand her the sock to hold, wipe fast, tape the fresh diaper down like wrapping a birthday present. It worked. He was so proud he almost carried the smell of victory straight to the kitchen, where Maya's lunch was waiting to be made. He stopped with one hand on the fridge handle. His mom had drilled him since he was five: after changing a diaper and before touching any food, twenty seconds of scrubbing with soap, no shortcuts. He had always thought the rule was just for little kids. Now, holding his hands under the light, he wondered exactly how long twenty seconds actually was.

He tried counting "one-Mississippi" but lost his place when Maya banged her spoon. Then he remembered the chorus of the song from the school talent show, the one Aubrey and Maximilian had performed while wearing dinosaur costumes. "Carnivores gotta wash their claws," he sang under his breath, working the soap between his fingers. He hummed the chorus once, then once more, because it was probable that one time wasn't a full twenty seconds. Two times felt right. Two times felt exactly right.

He texted the group chat: "Update: diaper disaster survived. Handwashing hack: hum the carnivore song twice at the sink and you're golden." Maximilian replied in seconds: "WAIT that's actually smart." Aubrey sent "claws up emoji" and a photo of the two of them in their dino costumes, which made Muhammad laugh so hard Maya laughed too, banging her spoon like a drum.

Maya ate her mashed banana with astonishing enthusiasm, slapping the tray between bites. Muhammad had just wiped her hands and face when his phone buzzed. A message from the neighbor glowed on the screen: "Home in ten minutes. Fair warning, Maya's older sister gets back from karate at the same time. She's six, she's loud, and she just learned the word carnivore. Good luck."

Muhammad looked at the front door, then at the spoon still in Maya's fist. From somewhere upstairs, a tooth was already rattling in a jar.
